summary:
Leviticus is nearly all direct speech — it opens, "Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting" (1:1) — and the whole book takes place camped at Sinai, spanning about a month by the Bible's own dating (Exodus 40:17; Numbers 1:1). The English title is Greek for "concerning the Levites," Levi being the tribe of Aaron's priestly family; the Hebrew title is the book's first word, vayikra, "and He called." Exodus ended with God's glory filling the tabernacle, Israel's tent sanctuary; Leviticus tells Israel how to live and worship beside it.

Chapters 1–7 set out five offerings: the burnt offering, given whole to God; the grain offering; the peace offering, eaten as a shared meal; and the sin and guilt offerings for wrongdoing. The reason for the blood is given in 17:11: "the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar" — "atonement" (Hebrew kipper) means purging or covering sin so that people can live near a holy God. Chapters 8–10 ordain Aaron and his sons as priests; two of them, Nadab and Abihu, offer "unauthorized fire" and die (10:1–2). Chapters 11–15 classify foods, childbirth, skin disease, and discharges as clean or unclean — ritual states, not sins, remedied by washing and waiting; the stated danger is "defiling My tabernacle" (15:31).

Chapter 16 institutes the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), the one day each year the high priest may enter the Most Holy Place, the innermost room, sprinkling blood on the mercy seat (the ark's gold cover) to cleanse the sanctuary of Israel's sins. He then confesses those sins over a live goat, the scapegoat, sent into the wilderness bearing "all their iniquities" (16:22). The Hebrew behind "scapegoat," azazel, is debated: "the goat that departs" or a proper name. Hebrews takes the rite as the pattern Jesus fulfills — the high priest entered "only once a year, and never without blood"; Christ entered "once for all by His own blood" (Hebrews 9:7, 12).

Chapters 17–26, often called the Holiness Code, carry holiness out of the sanctuary into daily life: wages paid on time, care for the poor and the foreigner, the festival calendar (23), and the Jubilee year, when ancestral land returns to its family (25). The keynote is "Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy" (19:2) — "holy" meaning set apart. The same chapter commands, "love your neighbor as yourself" (19:18), the line Jesus names the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:39) and Paul and James quote as the summary of the law (Galatians 5:14; James 2:8). Chapter 26 closes with blessings and curses: obedience brings rain and peace; rebellion ends in "I will scatter you among the nations" (26:33) — yet even then, "I will remember My covenant" (26:42), God's sworn bond with Abraham's line. The book signs off: "These are the commandments that the LORD gave to Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai" (27:34).
